Max Verstappen won the sprint race and followed up by securing pole position at the F1 Singapore Grand Prix, but Australia’s Oscar Piastri had to settle for seventh spot after an earlier collision with teammate Lando Norris in the sprint. Verstappen qualified first on the grid by 0.054 of a second ahead of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, with British veteran Lewis Hamilton third and F1 Championship leader Kimi Antonelli fourth. Besides Verstappen, the day’s other big winner was Antonelli, who widened his lead over George Russell when his Mercedes teammate crashed out from the lead in the sprint. Piastri’s McLaren teammate Lando Norris was fifth but they will be next to each other on row three in Sunday’s Grand Prix because of a penalty for Briton Russell. The two collided in the last lap of the sprint race fighting for fourth place, with Norris limping home in eighth and Piastri not finishing. World champion Norris apologised ‌to his McLaren team after the knock which saw him attempt an overtake but clipped the Australian’s rear tyre sending both cars spinning and handing Antonelli fourth place. “Sorry about that. Obviously I didn’t want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space ‌at the apex but ‌I was there,” ⁠Norris said over the team radio. While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the ​final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he became one of nine cars that did not finish - a record number of retirements for a Formula One sprint race. Piastri said he had not seen the incident but downplayed its significance as they were not in ‌high points ​scoring positions. “From where I sit, it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I’m not that bothered either way,” Piastri ​said. “Just obviously it’s ‌a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed (ahead of qualifying for Sunday’s race). Just a shame ​for the team.” Both McLaren drivers were summoned to meet the stewards after the collision but no further action was taken. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was not impressed with ​his drivers, however, adding that scoring just one point was not ‌enough. “Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable. This is something that we will discuss with our drivers,” he said. “We will do it in private. We will reiterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us. There’s no ego, there’s no person that is bigger than the interest of the McLaren Formula One team.” Russell beat Verstappen off the line at the start in wet conditions but lost control when he put a wheel on a painted line at the end of the first lap, spinning across the track and into the barrier. Antonelli was fourth, extending his lead over Russell from 84 points to 89, after he picked up two positions on the last lap when Norris and Piastri collided ahead of him. Russell has a grid penalty for Sunday’s Grand Prix, meaning the 20-year-old Antonelli could take another big step toward becoming F1’s youngest-ever champion. items.article_search_text: Lando Norris and his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri crashed on the final lap of the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint; the incident cost McLaren eight championship points; watch Sundays Singapore Grand Prix at 1pm (build-up from 11.30am) live on Sky Sports F1 Lando Norris has revealed he was "told off" by McLaren following a collision with team-mate Oscar Piastri during the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint that team principal Andrea Stella said was "not acceptable". Norris had narrowly trailed Piastri in a battle for fourth for most of the 20-lap race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where overtaking is extremely difficult. Norris tried to go up the inside of Turn 5 on the final circuit, which led to a crash as Piastri turned in, with the Australian spun around as his rear-right tyre was struck by his team-mate's front-left. Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 Piastri suffered damage that took him out of the race, while Norris was able to get going again and take the chequered flag in eighth for the final point. After summoning the drivers for a hearing, the stewards decided not to take any action as they deemed that both had contributed to the collision. However, the general consensus in the paddock was that Norris, who had been trailing and attempted the pass, was more responsible. Norris initially insisted he believed the pass had been on, but speaking later on Saturday following qualifying and discussions with Piastri and the McLaren hierarchy, he told Sky Sports F1 : "As a team we all spoke about it. I apologised but that's all you need to know." Pushed by Sky Italy for details of the discussions, he added: "I was told off." Piastri retained a calm outlook on the incident, but said: "It was clear those kind of things can't happen. Everyone knows where we sit. "We will all be fine and keep pushing together like we always do." Stella: Incident simply not acceptable McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said the incident was "not acceptable" but chose not to single out either of his drivers for criticism. "It's been a long day," Stella told Sky Sports F1 . "The Sprint race was a race that was giving us some good points, in a moment in which we are not in condition to win. Still, we were in condition to score good points. "And we saw two McLarens having contact, basically going out of the race. Lando could score one point but definitely that's not enough. "Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable. "This is something that we will discuss with our drivers. We will do it in private. We will reiterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us. There's no ego, there's no person that's bigger than the interest of the McLaren F1 team. This will be reiterated. "I'm sure, like always, there will be conversations that will lead to the team being more united and even stronger." Brundle: Not smart from Norris The move Norris attempted was "not smart", according to Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle. Speaking on commentary immediately after the incident, Brundle said: "McLaren will be furious about that, on the final lap of a Sprint. "Whether they were fourth or fifth, it would have made no difference to the team whatsoever." The difference between finishing fourth and fifth in a Sprint is only one point. McLaren were on course to collect nine points, but instead ended up taking just one and seeing their lead over Red Bull in the battle for third in the constructors' standings cut to just 11 points. Brundle suggested that reigning world champion Norris was largely responsible for the collision. "That was not smart, Lando. That was not smart at all," Brundle said. "I think Lando got on the kerb on the inside as the space pinched a little bit and that slid him even more into the side of his team-mate. "It just wasn't worth the risk. What was Oscar going to do? I know they're racers. It just wasn't worth taking the risk just to swap the two cars around in a Sprint." Norris insists pass was on Norris immediately apologised to his team over the radio but insisted in his post-session interview that he thought the move was on. The Brit said over team radio: "Sorry about that. Obviously I didn't want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex but I was there, so..." Quizzed over the incident in his post-race interview with Sky Sports F1 , Norris added: "I'd rather just go back and review it." On whether he still believed "the move was on", Norris said: "It was." Piastri played down the incident, claiming he wasn't "that bothered" due to the fact it was a Sprint event. "I've not seen it properly," the Australian told Sky Sports F1 . "From where I sit, I'm not...it's for fourth and fifth for a Sprint race so I'm not that bothered either way. Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed. "Just a shame for the team." 'A hell of a lunge' Sky Sports F1 pundit and former world champion Jenson Button described Norris' move as "a hell of a lunge". Reflecting on Norris' comments after the incident, Button said: "He was very bullish. Normally when you're that bullish, you're being defensive. "It was a hell of a lunge. On your team-mate, at that moment in a race. "And the problem is the corner does tighten quite a lot at the apex and he found himself in the side of his team-mate." items.article_search_text: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri's collision at the end of the Singapore sprint race went unpunished by Formula 1's stewards, who declared "both drivers had contributed to the incident." Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s collision at the end of the Singapore sprint race went unpunished by Formula 1’s stewards, who declared “both drivers had contributed to the incident.” Norris tried a late and optimistic pass on his McLaren teammate down the inside of Turn 5 on the final lap, but collided as Piastri moved across to take the corner himself. The McLaren drivers had been running fourth and fifth when the incident occurred. McLaren’s rules of on-track engagement was one of the biggest Formula 1 storylines of the past two years -- infamously dubbed ‘Papaya Rules’ by team boss Andrea Stella in 2024, a nod to the papaya shade of orange on the team’s cars. Saturday’s collision took Piastri out of the race completely, although Norris recovered to finish eighth, collecting a single point in the process. Norris seemed irritated when asked about the move afterwards by Viaplay. Asked if it was unnecessary, he replied: “What, to go for a big gap? Or overtake?” He then asked the journalist: “What’s the title of the race? Sprint ... What’s after sprint?” When the journalist replied “race,” Norris replied: “Wow, good job. Yeah, it’s race!” The stewards deemed neither driver was predominantly to blame. In a verdict released just as qualifying for Sunday’s grand prix started, the stewards said both could have avoided the incident which occurred. The statement read: “The driver of Car 81 explained that he had not expected Car 1 to attempt an overtake and, after turning in, noticed Car 1 on the inside and attempted to leave space. The driver of Car 1 said that he saw an opportunity to overtake. He said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of Car 81 prior to the apex and therefore expected to be left space. “As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated so he had to use the inside kerb and braked and a collision occurred. The Stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision. Therefore the Stewards determined to take no further action.”

items.article_search_text: Lando Norris learns the stewards’ verdict on Oscar Piastri’s nightmare crash, as the incident raises questions about the race. Norris escapes a penalty after the Singapore Sprint clash. Piastri’s race ends at Turn 5. The stewards blame neither McLaren driver outright. Lando Norris has escaped punishment after his final-lap collision with Oscar Piastri in the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint, with the F1 stewards ruling that both drivers contributed to the crash. The verdict closes a tense crash investigation into a move that ended one car’s race and spun the other away from a likely points haul. Piastri was running fourth when Norris launched an inside attack at Turn 5. Their McLarens made contact at the apex, sending both off track; Piastri hit the barrier and retired, while Norris recovered to finish eighth and score one point. For McLaren, the incident transformed a potential fourth-and-fifth finish worth nine points into a single point. The stewards’ verdict: no penalty decision and no further action. Singapore Sprint crash investigation: what happened at Turn 5 Norris saw a passing opportunity on the final lap and committed to the inside line. He told the stewards that his front axle had moved ahead of Piastri’s mirror before the apex, leading him to expect room on the inside. As the gap narrowed, Norris used the kerb and braked, but his left-front tyre clipped Piastri’s right-rear. Piastri said he did not expect his team-mate to attack there. After turning into the corner, he spotted the orange car and tried to leave space, but the contact sent both cars into a spin. The Australian struck the barrier and retired on the spot; Norris rejoined and brought his damaged car home in eighth. The sequence was abrupt, but the stewards’ account points to a shared misjudgement rather than a one-sided hit. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vJhdzK3uO7qg F1 stewards explain the penalty decision The stewards reviewed video and in-car footage, then heard from both drivers and team representatives. Their finding was that Norris attempted the overtake and misjudged how much room remained, while Piastri also contributed as he turned into the corner. Neither driver, the report concluded, carried sole or predominant responsibility. That distinction explains why the stewards’ verdict stopped short of a penalty. A collision does not automatically trigger a sanction; the officials weighed the positioning, the available space and each driver’s account. The outcome differs from other close calls, such as the Leclerc-Piastri collision debate, where the circumstances and driver assessments shaped the story. Here, the ruling leaves both McLaren racers without an official penalty. What the Singapore verdict means for McLaren The result carries a blunt sporting cost: McLaren lost eight points against the nine-point return its cars appeared set to secure, while Norris salvaged one. The official ruling protects both drivers from a penalty, but it does not erase the damage to the team’s Sprint tally or the lost chance to convert a strong position into a double points finish. For Norris and Piastri, the immediate work is internal: review the onboard footage, agree how they judge space in a late-race fight, and avoid turning a shared error into a wider team fault line. The stewards’ call settles the formal case; McLaren still has to manage the sporting fallout. Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race after George Russell crashed out from the lead, missing a chance to cut his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli's advantage in the hunt for the Formula One title. In a chaotic race on Saturday that also saw Lando Norris collide with his McLaren teammate, Australia's Oscar Piastri, Russell beat Verstappen off the line at the start in wet conditions but lost control when he put a wheel on a painted line at the end of the first lap, spinning across the track and into the barrier. The British driver tapped his hands against the car in frustration as he climbed out. "I'm fine. Sorry, sorry, sorry," he told Mercedes over the radio. Verstappen eased to the win after that, backing up his victory in Malaysia last week, with Ferrari duo Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc second and third. Antonelli was fourth, extending his lead over Russell from 84 points to 89, after he picked up two positions on the last lap when Norris and Piastri collided ahead of him. Norris tried an ambitious overtake down the inside of his teammate but badly misjudged it and sent the Australian spinning into the barrier. McLaren chief executive Zak Brown shook his head in dismay on the pit wall. Russell has a grid penalty for Sunday's Grand Prix, meaning the 20-year-old Antonelli could take another big step towards becoming F1's youngest-ever champion. Russell wasn't the only driver to be caught out in the wet conditions. He was one of eight non-finishers after a spate of collisions and technical problems, with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar stopped by car trouble. Verstappen said Red Bull will need to work on its "horrendous" starts after he lost the lead off the line, just as he did in Malaysia last week. "We don't accelerate off the line," he said. "Up until now we always have terrible starts, so we need to understand what's going on there." New Zealander Liam Lawson was fifth for Racing Bulls, with Haas's Oliver Bearman sixth and Nico Hulkenberg seventh for Audi. Norris recovered to claim a point in eighth in the last sprint of 2026. The start was delayed because of heavy rain, making it the second week running that an F1 race has started late. Last week's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was first held up by a downpour, then because several cars' software failed to cope with the wet conditions. The FIA issued a software update that was also being used in Singapore this week. Qualifying is later on Saturday for the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday. Australian Associated Press

However, on the final lap of the race, Lando Norris collided with his teammate, Oscar Piastri , at Turn 5, whilst the duo were running in fourth and fifth, with Piastri in the lead car. After the incident, Norris was able to get going again and crossed the line in eighth place, securing one point for the team. The British driver is now under investigation by the FIA and will have to report to the stewards before qualifying. But on the other side of the garage, Piastri was not able to finish the sprint race and was one of the nine drivers who failed to finish the 20-lap sprint. Immediately after the race, the reigning F1 world champion was asked about his point of view on the collision. “I'd rather just go back and review it,” Norris told Sky Sports. When asked if the move was on, Norris said, “It was… I apologize to them that one of the cars is out, but like I said, the rest of it we'll go review." On the other side of the incident, Piastri, who was leading his teammate, ended up with nothing to show from the sprint race. The Australian driver had not seen the incident again when he spoke to the media, and was more interested in the amount of work that the team would have to do before the Grand Prix qualifying session. “I've not seen it properly. I mean, from where I sit, it's fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so not that bothered either way,” Piastri admitted. “Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed, so, just a shame for the team.” Due to the delays caused by the weather conditions ahead of the sprint race, there are further delays to the qualifying session later in the day. These delays will give McLaren time to get Norris and Piastri’s cars ready for the chance to get decent grid slots for the Grand Prix on Sunday. Several other drivers are also under investigation. 10th October 2026, 11:43 10th October 2026, 16:26 | Written by Keith Collantine The stewards have taken no action against the McLaren drivers over their last-lap collision in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race. Advert | Become a Supporter & go ad-free Lando Norris attempted to dive down the inside of Oscar Piastri at turn five. The pair were following Charles Leclerc’s third-placed Ferrari at the time. The McLarens made contact at the apex of the corner. Both spun and Piastri hit the barrier on the outside. Norris was able to continue and finish in eighth place. “Sorry about that,” Norris told his team on the radio. “Obviously I didn’t want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex but I was there.” Afterwards Norris defended his decision to attempt the pass where he did, insisting it was a viable move. “In the last lap there was a big opportunity into [turn] five so I went for it,” he said. “The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I’ve had to back out of it because the gap was closing. “So I’ve tried to avoid the incident and obviously there still was one, but it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team.” Piastri played down the collision. “From where I sit, it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race so I’m not that bothered either way,” he said. “Just obviously it’s a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed.” Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free After examining the incident and speaking to both drivers, the stewards decided not to penalise them. Two other drivers were cleared following investigations. Alexander Albon was investigated for driving in the wrong direction after spinning during the Safety Car period and Oliver Bearman was investigated for driving unnecessarily slowly. The stewards decided Sergio Perez was responsible for his clash with Lance Stroll and ruled a five-second time penalty was deserved. However as he did not finish the race, no penalty was applied. The stewards also took issued no penalty over another incident involving Alexander Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas. As in Perez’s case, Bottas was found to deserve a penalty, but received none because he retired. The driver of car one [Norris] attempted to overtake car 81 [Piastri] on the inside at turn five. A collision occurred at the apex. The driver of car 81 explained that he had not expected car one to attempt an overtake and, after turning in, noticed car one on the inside and attempted to leave space. The driver of car one said that he saw an opportunity to overtake. He said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of car 81 prior to the apex and therefore expected to be left space. As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated so he had to use the inside kerb and braked and a collision occurred. The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision. Therefore the stewards determined to take no further action. Car 11 [Perez] attempted to overtake car 18 [Stroll] on the inside into turn 16 and both cars made contact. The stewards determine that the driver of car 18 took a reasonable line into the corner and therefore was not at fault. Car 11 attempted to overtake car 18 on the inside into turn 16 and both cars made contact. The stewards determine that the driver of car 11 initiated the overtaking attempt in a legitimate way, but then locked up the front right wheel therefore was not able to rotate the car anymore. The stewards determine the the driver of car 11 was predominantly at fault, but also take into account the weather conditions and acknowledge the difficulties of controlling the car on the brakes in such circumstances. Therefore a five-second time penalty is deemed appropriate and would have been applied in-race if that had been possible. As car 11 was not classified and five-second time penalties regularly do not convert into grid drops, no penalty is applied in this case. The stewards thoroughly reviewed marshalling/positioning data, timing data and on- board cameras. The driver concerned stayed at or above speeds necessary to stay below 1:52.0 around the vast majority of the circuit. However, the stewards determined that the drivers took appropriate actions to not impede other drivers, and slowed down significantly to allow another driver to pass while giving this driver a clear track. The stewards therefore determine that the driver concerned did not drive “unnecessarily slowly”, and that he was above the maximum time because he took appropriate steps, and we therefore take no further action. Car 41 [Lindblad] spun after the exit of turn five and was facing towards oncoming cars. Car 41 drove in the wrong direction for approximately 100 metres back to turn five and used the run-off area to turn around. The driver explained that he could not perform a flick turn from the position in which his car was stopped after the spin. Because he was facing the wrong way, he drove back a short distance against oncoming traffic but staying to the edge of the track and away from the racing line. After he was sure the last car had passed, the driver of car 41 attempted a flick turn but the car would not rotate. The driver explained that, knowing that the last car had passed and it would present no danger for him to continue, he drove back to turn five where he knew there would be space to turn. Having regard to the difficult position the driver of car 41 found himself in, where his car was originally prone and then unable to turn, and given further that there was no oncoming traffic, the stewards determined that what occurred was not in these circumstances unsafe and therefore took no further action. When preparing for the restart at the end of a Safety Car period, car 23 collided with the rear of car 5, and car 77 collided with the rear of car 23. The driver of car 77 said that he had no opportunity to avoid colliding with the rear of car 23 after car 23 checked-up after it collided with car 5. In the Stewards’ assessment both collisions were a consequence of a concertina created by cars ahead travelling at inconsistent speeds in the preparation for the restart. As cars 23 and 77 were towards the back of the pack of slow moving cars, the chain reaction effect on them was more pronounced. Nonetheless, the stewards determined that like the collision between cars 23 and 5, the collision between cars 77 and 23 could have been avoided had the driver of car 77 recognised the risk of a concertina ahead and left more space when following car 23, particularly having regard to the damp conditions. Had car 77 not retired from the sprint as a consequence of the collision, the stewards would have imposed a 5 second time penalty rather than the usual 10 second time penalty taking into account that, in part at least, a number of cars ahead in the queue had contributed by slowing at inconsistent rates. A 5 second time penalty would not have been converted into a grid penalty and therefore the Stewards determined not to apply a penalty in this case. items.article_search_text: The FIA has admitted a bad fault that saw a crucial setting switched on and off accidentally. 7NEWS brings you the latest local news from Australia and around the world. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS. Max Verstappen has lit up the streets of Singapore to pip George Russell to sprint pole while Australian hope Oscar Piastri forced his way into fourth place. The action was overshadowed when the cars’ settings were wrongly changed by race control, affecting the cars and blamed for some drivers being eliminated from the session early. Verstappen who claimed his first win of the F1 season at the Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia last weekend, was in imperious form again as his Red Bull showed further signs of progress. “It is always close in Singapore, your lap — you are pushing as close as you can to the walls. I did not expect this, very happy to be first,” Verstappen said. Russell saved his best until last but was unable to topple the four-time world champion, finishing 0.120 seconds adrift as he bumped Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc down to third. Piastri claimed fourth for Saturday’s 21-lap dash, ahead of McLaren teammate Lando Norris and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton. Runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli was off the pace throughout the session and could manage only seventh – 0.693sec off the pace to raise further doubts over the upgrade Mercedes brought last weekend. Antonelli has one hand on the title after team-mate Russell’s power-unit failure in the closing stages last week gave the Italian an 84-point lead with just seven rounds to run. Russell, running the Mercedes car without the upgrade, will start the main race on Sunday from the back of the grid after taking a new power unit, in a further blow to his slender title hopes. Verstappen was summoned by the stewards in an investigation into whether he overtook Lewis Hamilton earlier in the qualifying session under yellow flags, but he was not penalised. Cars were down on power for several minutes in the first part of Friday’s qualifying session because “overtake mode” — an electrical power boost activated by the drivers — was disabled. Williams team principal James Vowles said the issue played a role in both of his drivers being eliminated, with Alex Albon 19th and Carlos Sainz, Jr. 22nd. The FIA blamed “a human error in race control” which meant cars were blocked from using overtake mode after the session was briefly red-flagged. The setting was then switched back on for 27 seconds, and switched off again. “The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap,” the governing body said. It’s the latest in a series of issues with the software which governs the 2026 cars’ electrical power and comes five days after cars crawled to a halt in the rain in Malaysia, delaying the race start. Leclerc led Hamilton in a Ferrari one-two in a second session delayed by 16 minutes after Verstappen had topped the first, to hint at an open fight for pole. So it proved but it was Verstappen who pulled the stellar lap out the bag in the closing stages and the four-time world champion will hope to continue his step forward with sprint victory on Saturday. Dutchman Max Verstappen has delivered a wet weather masterclass, executing a flawless drive to win a rain-soaked delayed race in Sepang, with Piastri in sixth. Thanks for joining us everyone. Goodnight and we’ll see you next time “It doesn’t matter how good of a racing driver you are, if you can’t see where you’re going”. Those were the simple, but wise words from veteran F1 commentator Martin Brundle moments before the rain-delayed Bahrain Grand Prix tried to start, had to stop and then finally started again. Held in Malaysia’s Sepang International Circuit in Kuala Lumpur – after the conflict in the Middle East cancelled the Bahrain race – the grand prix had all the ingredients of a chaotic race. It was the first wet race of the season under the new regulations and new cars. Plus Sepang had not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017, meaning more than half the grid were unfamiliar with the track. Cue carnage. Ultimately, it was Max Verstappen who rose above it all, delivering a wet weather masterclass and winning the grand prix after a 90-minute delay due to poor weather. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished in second with Lewis Hamilton snatching third, after a power unit issue ended George Russell’s race with five laps to go. Sunday was Verstappen’s first race win since Abu Dhabi in 2025. “It’s a really nice one [win] after the year we’ve had and the progression we have made,” he said in a post race interview “I’m incredibly proud of everyone. Just super nice to win here.” For at least 90-minute it looked like the grand prix might not happen, as heavy downpour turned the Sepang circuit into a lake. Drivers attempted to do formation laps, but complained the track was still too damp and dangerous, so the FIA opted to wait and then do a standing start. A crash into the gravel from Valtteri Bottas triggered a safety car, providing the perfect opportunity for Verstappen to snatch the lead from Antonelli (who overtook him on the opening lap). From there Verstappen scarcely looked back and seemed untouchable building a 10 plus second lead to his rivals. A last-minute safety car (triggered by a crash from Alex Albon, compounded by car issues for Russell) suddenly eradicated Verstappen’s lead and gave Antonelli an opportunity to snatch the lead with five laps to go. But Verstappen held on to win – securing a much-needed victory for Red Bull this year. Despite some fantastic overtakes and battles with Kiwi Liam Lawson, Oscar Piastri started and finished the race in sixth. The luckless Australian was on the wrong side of safety car timings and pitstops and couldn’t finish higher. Arguably Russell had a much worse day. The Mercedes driver notched his third DNF this season after being consistently plagued by power unit issues. “So many times this season it happened... It’s a real shame, but you’ve got to keep fighting,” he said. There are still seven grands prix left, but Antonelli appears to be a champion in waiting. Dutchman Max Verstappen has delivered a wet weather masterclass, executing a flawless drive to win a rain-soaked race in Sepang that was delayed by 90 minutes. The Red Bull champion navigating a flurry of pit stops, safety cars and wet weather carnage to claim the trophy, with Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton rounding out the podium. This is Verstappen’s first race win in 2026 after a challenging year with Red Bull. His last one occurred in back in December. Sepang has not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017. Ironically, the winner that year was Max Verstappen, which means the Dutchman has now won both races consecutively (just with a nine-year gap). Oscar Piastri started the race and finished the race in sixth. Despite delivering some fantastic moments including a nail-biting fight with Liam Lawson, the Australian was unable to finish higher and was unlucky with pitstop timings. Lewis Hamilton has fought his way back the back of the grid after a horrible start and is now on the podium. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen is still leading but Antonelli is right there with him. Oh dear, That is devastating news for George Russell. His Mercedes has suffered a power unit with five laps to go. Lando Norris is also into the gravel and has plummeted down the ladder into 11th place. The safety car is about to end and we have four laps to go. When it lifts, it’s basically going to be a sprint. Verstappen leads the pack but Kimi Antonelli is directly behind him. George Russell is out of the race, which means Hadjar is now in third with Hamilton in fourth. Marshalls are having trouble removing Albon’s smashed car and a full safety car has now been deployed. Mercedes have a chance to attack Verstappen for the lead. The Dutchman’s 10-second lead is gone. Oscar Piastri, who didn’t pit during the earlier virtual safety car, is now a sitting duck for those around him. Luckily, McLaren bring both Piastri and Lando Norris in for fresh tyres. Max Verstappen has pretty much already won this race. Which means the broadcaster (Sky Sports) isn’t showing much of his race. Instead, commentators are focusing on the battle between Hamilton and Hadjar who are fighting for fifth place. BUT WAIT Alex Albon is stopped on the side of the track, after suffering a gearbox failure. This triggers a virtual safety car and Antonelli manages to sneak past him. But Mercedes call the Italian in moments later and Verstappen regains the lead. Lewis Hamilton has found himself right onto the rear wing of Isack Hadjar, and is trying to snatch fourth place. Meanwhile, Oscar Piastri is marooned in seventh, after encountering some traffic after his pitstop. The Australian started in sixth so let’s hope he’s able to move up a few more places.

items.article_search_text: The race starts at 6pm AEDT and is being held in Malaysia after the Bahrain Grand Prix was cancelled in April because of conflict in the Middle East. Dutchman Max Verstappen has delivered a wet weather masterclass, executing a flawless drive to win a rain-soaked delayed race in Sepang, with Piastri in sixth. Thanks for joining us everyone. Goodnight and we’ll see you next time “It doesn’t matter how good of a racing driver you are, if you can’t see where you’re going”. Those were the simple, but wise words from veteran F1 commentator Martin Brundle moments before the rain-delayed Bahrain Grand Prix tried to start, had to stop and then finally started again. Held in Malaysia’s Sepang International Circuit in Kuala Lumpur – after the conflict in the Middle East cancelled the Bahrain race – the grand prix had all the ingredients of a chaotic race. It was the first wet race of the season under the new regulations and new cars. Plus Sepang had not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017, meaning more than half the grid were unfamiliar with the track. Cue carnage. Ultimately, it was Max Verstappen who rose above it all, delivering a wet weather masterclass and winning the grand prix after a 90-minute delay due to poor weather. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished in second with Lewis Hamilton snatching third, after a power unit issue ended George Russell’s race with five laps to go. Sunday was Verstappen’s first race win since Abu Dhabi in 2025. “It’s a really nice one [win] after the year we’ve had and the progression we have made,” he said in a post race interview “I’m incredibly proud of everyone. Just super nice to win here.” For at least 90-minute it looked like the grand prix might not happen, as heavy downpour turned the Sepang circuit into a lake. Drivers attempted to do formation laps, but complained the track was still too damp and dangerous, so the FIA opted to wait and then do a standing start. A crash into the gravel from Valtteri Bottas triggered a safety car, providing the perfect opportunity for Verstappen to snatch the lead from Antonelli (who overtook him on the opening lap). From there Verstappen scarcely looked back and seemed untouchable building a 10 plus second lead to his rivals. A last-minute safety car (triggered by a crash from Alex Albon, compounded by car issues for Russell) suddenly eradicated Verstappen’s lead and gave Antonelli an opportunity to snatch the lead with five laps to go. But Verstappen held on to win – securing a much-needed victory for Red Bull this year. Despite some fantastic overtakes and battles with Kiwi Liam Lawson, Oscar Piastri started and finished the race in sixth. The luckless Australian was on the wrong side of safety car timings and pitstops and couldn’t finish higher. Arguably Russell had a much worse day. The Mercedes driver notched his third DNF this season after being consistently plagued by power unit issues. “So many times this season it happened... It’s a real shame, but you’ve got to keep fighting,” he said. There are still seven grands prix left, but Antonelli appears to be a champion in waiting. Dutchman Max Verstappen has delivered a wet weather masterclass, executing a flawless drive to win a rain-soaked race in Sepang that was delayed by 90 minutes. The Red Bull champion navigating a flurry of pit stops, safety cars and wet weather carnage to claim the trophy, with Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton rounding out the podium. This is Verstappen’s first race win in 2026 after a challenging year with Red Bull. His last one occurred in back in December. Sepang has not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017. Ironically, the winner that year was Max Verstappen, which means the Dutchman has now won both races consecutively (just with a nine-year gap). Oscar Piastri started the race and finished the race in sixth. Despite delivering some fantastic moments including a nail-biting fight with Liam Lawson, the Australian was unable to finish higher and was unlucky with pitstop timings. Lewis Hamilton has fought his way back the back of the grid after a horrible start and is now on the podium. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen is still leading but Antonelli is right there with him. Verstappen is flying and is showing no signs of letting anyone get past him. Piastri gets on the inside, but Liam Lawson roars alongside him. Piastri snatches it back swiftly to reclaim 6th place. Kimi Antonelli is still holding on to second and the clock is ticking down. HERE COMES LEWIS HAMILTON The seven-time world champion gets passed Hadjar, triggered a gigantic cheer from the crowd. Oh dear, That is devastating news for George Russell. His Mercedes has suffered a power unit with five laps to go. Lando Norris is also into the gravel and has plummeted down the ladder into 11th place. The safety car is about to end and we have four laps to go. When it lifts, it’s basically going to be a sprint. Verstappen leads the pack but Kimi Antonelli is directly behind him. George Russell is out of the race, which means Hadjar is now in third with Hamilton in fourth. Marshalls are having trouble removing Albon’s smashed car and a full safety car has now been deployed. Mercedes have a chance to attack Verstappen for the lead. The Dutchman’s 10-second lead is gone. Oscar Piastri, who didn’t pit during the earlier virtual safety car, is now a sitting duck for those around him. Luckily, McLaren bring both Piastri and Lando Norris in for fresh tyres. Max Verstappen has pretty much already won this race. Which means the broadcaster (Sky Sports) isn’t showing much of his race. Instead, commentators are focusing on the battle between Hamilton and Hadjar who are fighting for fifth place. BUT WAIT Alex Albon is stopped on the side of the track, after suffering a gearbox failure. This triggers a virtual safety car and Antonelli manages to sneak past him. But Mercedes call the Italian in moments later and Verstappen regains the lead. Lewis Hamilton has found himself right onto the rear wing of Isack Hadjar, and is trying to snatch fourth place. Meanwhile, Oscar Piastri is marooned in seventh, after encountering some traffic after his pitstop. The Australian started in sixth so let’s hope he’s able to move up a few more places.
